meta.description: Voltaire really wrote it — but about a government minister, not 'every man.' The line is from The Age of Louis XIV (1751); the popular version is a paraphrase.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Every man is guilty of all the good he did not do'?
meta.ogDescription: Yes, it's Voltaire — but he aimed it at ministers of state. The Age of Louis XIV (1751) reads 'guilty of all the good he does not do'; the short form is a paraphrase.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1694–1778 · French Enlightenment writer, historian and philosophe
answer.sourceLine: Voltaire really did write this — but about a minister of state, not “every man.” The line comes from his history Le Siècle de Louis XIV (1751): “in the calm he is guilty of all the good he does not do.” The familiar universal wording is a later paraphrase that broadens his point about those who hold power.

source.heading: Voltaire on the duty of a minister

docMeta.dd: Le Siècle de Louis XIV (The Age of Louis XIV)
Chapter on the state of France to the death of Cardinal Mazarin (1661)
A generalized paraphrase — not Voltaire’s exact words

source.excerpt: A minister of state is excusable for the harm he does when the helm of government has forced his hand in a storm; but in the calm he is guilty of all the good he does not do.
trail: Wikiquote lists the full sentence as sourced to Le Siècle de Louis XIV ↗ and notes “Every man is guilty of all the good he did not do” as an unsourced paraphrase or variant translation.
The scholarly Littré dictionary ↗ quotes the French original and cites it to “Louis XIV, 6.”
Popular quote sites such as The Quotations Page ↗ carry the short “Every man…” form with no primary source at all.
source.cutTag: ↑ Voltaire wrote ‘a minister of state’ — the popular version swaps in ‘every man’
source.excerptNote: Voltaire’s point is about those who hold power: in a crisis a minister may be forgiven the harm forced on him, but in calm times he answers for the good he fails to do. The original French reads “Un ministre… il est coupable de tout le bien qu’il ne fait pas.”

source.rightsNote: Voltaire died in 1778 and Le Siècle de Louis XIV (1751) is long in the public domain; the popular English paraphrase is likewise free to quote.

author.metaLine: 1694–1778 · French Enlightenment writer, historian and philosophe
author.bio: Voltaire was the pen name of François-Marie Arouet, one of the leading writers of the French Enlightenment, celebrated for his wit, his campaigns against intolerance and injustice, and works from Candide to his histories. Le Siècle de Louis XIV (1751), where this line appears, was a pioneering “history of civilization” in which he judged rulers and ministers by the good they achieved — or failed to.

misattribution.heading: A real quote, quietly rewritten
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Voltaire is correct — the distortion is in the words. Voltaire wrote about a government minister in a specific political setting; the popular version silently promotes the remark to a universal moral law about everyone.

items.scope: Generalized from Voltaire’s actual line about
items.why: Voltaire’s sentence in Le Siècle de Louis XIV ↗ reads “a minister of state… is guilty of all the good he does not do” — a judgment on those who wield power, not on every person. The French original (“Un ministre…”) is confirmed by the Littré dictionary ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are genuinely Voltaire’s, but he aimed them at ministers of state, not at mankind at large — per Wikiquote ↗ and Littré ↗.

context.heading: Why the wording matters
lead: The full sentence is a piece of political ethics, not a personal self-help maxim. Voltaire draws a line between two situations: a minister forced by crisis (“the helm of government… in a storm”) may be excused the harm he causes, but in calm times he is fully answerable for the good he neglects.

Stripped to “Every man is guilty of all the good he did not do,” the line loses that context and becomes a sweeping charge against everyone — which is why it now circulates on posters and in graduation speeches far from its original subject.
detailsBody: In Le Siècle de Louis XIV Voltaire applies the thought to Cardinal Mazarin, adding that Mazarin “did good to no one but himself and those related to him.” The remark is part of his broader project of judging statesmen by their record.

The generalization to “every man” appears to have entered circulation through English translations and quotation collections, where it is repeated without the surrounding sentence about ministers and storms.
context.pull: He aimed it at those who hold power — not at everyone.
